DOCUMENT:
Menu Pricing Review: Spring 2026
The Copper Kettle, prepared by the General Manager for the owners, March 2026

1. Purpose
This paper reviews main-course pricing and menu mix and proposes changes to take effect with the spring menu on 1 April 2026. Our overall gross margin on food, across all courses, has slipped from 70% to 67% over the past year as ingredient costs have risen faster than our prices, and we last changed main-course prices in September 2024.

2. Trading pattern
The Copper Kettle is a 64-cover restaurant open for lunch and dinner from Wednesday to Sunday. We serve an average of 1,050 main courses a week, with Friday and Saturday dinner accounting for just under half. Our customers are mainly local, with a strong repeat base: our booking system shows that around 60% of bookings come from guests who have dined with us in the past six months.

Table 1. Main courses, average weekly sales (January-February 2026)
Dish | Menu price | Food cost per plate | Gross margin | Plates per week
Fish and chips | £16.50 | £5.10 | 69% | 310
Beef burger | £15.00 | £4.20 | 72% | 260
Chicken curry | £14.50 | £3.60 | 75% | 180
Sirloin steak | £26.00 | £10.40 | 60% | 120
Mushroom risotto | £14.00 | £2.80 | 80% | 90
Other mains (specials) | various | various | 64% | 90

3. Competitor prices
We checked menus at the five restaurants we regard as our closest competitors. Their fish and chips ranges from £16.95 to £19.00, burgers from £15.50 to £17.50 and sirloin steak from £27.00 to £32.00. Our prices for these three dishes are the lowest in the group.

4. Supplier costs
Our meat supplier has given notice that beef prices will rise by 12% from 1 April 2026, reflecting national cattle prices. Other supplier prices are expected to be broadly stable over the spring. Fish prices have been volatile but are currently close to their 2025 average.

5. Proposals
5.1 Price increases. Raise fish and chips to £17.50, the beef burger to £16.00 and the sirloin steak to £28.00. All three would remain below the midpoint of the competitor range for that dish.

5.2 Remove the mushroom risotto. Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place. We propose replacing it with a seasonal vegetarian special at the same price.

5.3 Projected effect. If volumes hold, the price increases add £1.00 per plate on 310 fish and chips, £1.00 on 260 burgers and £2.00 on 120 steaks, a total of £810 a week in additional gross profit, or £42,120 a year. Because our prices remain competitive and our customer base is loyal, we expect volumes to hold. The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target.

6. Communication
Menus will be reprinted for 1 April. Staff will be briefed on the changes, and we will not draw attention to the increases on the menu. We will monitor plates sold per dish weekly for the first eight weeks against the January to February baseline.

7. Risks
Some regular guests may notice the increases. However, the last price change in 2024 had no visible effect on bookings, and the new prices remain competitive. Weekday lunch trade is more price-sensitive than dinner, but it represents a small share of main-course sales.

8. Recommendation
We recommend that the owners approve the three price increases and the replacement of the mushroom risotto from 1 April 2026. Together these changes add about £42,000 a year in gross profit, improve our margin and keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [misread_evidence] at: "Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place." -- Table 1 shows mushroom risotto has the highest gross margin on the menu (80%); the weakest is sirloin steak (60%). Lowest sales is correct (90 plates, tied with specials), but the margin claim misreads the table.
2. [missing_consideration] at: "The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target." -- The projection uses current food costs, but section 4 states beef prices rise 12% from 1 April, the same date as the new prices. Burgers and steaks (380 plates a week) would see higher food costs (e.g. about £1.25 more per steak), eroding much of the projected gain; the margin and profit projections never account for it.
3. [inconsistency] at: "keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week" -- Section 2 says the restaurant is open Wednesday to Sunday, i.e. five days a week; the recommendation refers to six trading days.

REVIEW:
# Review: Menu Pricing Review, Spring 2026

The paper proposes three price rises: fish and chips £16.50 → £17.50, burger £15.00 → £16.00 and sirloin £26.00 → £28.00. It projects £810 a week (£42,120 a year) in extra gross profit and a main-course margin of about 71%. It also proposes replacing the mushroom risotto, on the grounds that it has the weakest margin and lowest sales.

**Much of the arithmetic is correct:**
- **Margins:** every margin in Table 1 follows from its price and food cost.
- **Volumes:** plates sum to 1,050 a week.
- **Weekly gain:** £310 + £260 + £240 = £810, and £810 × 52 = £42,120.
- **Competitors:** each new price is below the midpoint of the competitor range (£17.98, £16.50, £29.50).

The pricing logic is reasonable. But the risotto decision is based on a misreading of Table 1, and the projected gain ignores two costs the paper itself raises.

## 1. The risotto has the *highest* margin on the menu

Table 1 shows the risotto at **80%**, the highest on the menu. The *lowest* is the sirloin at 60%. Its sales of 90 plates are joint lowest with specials, so that part is true.

The proposal also makes margin worse, not better. It replaces an 80% dish with a seasonal special, and specials currently run at **64%**. On current volumes that costs roughly £200 a week in gross profit, about a quarter of the gain from the price rises.

The risotto also appears to be **the only vegetarian main**. A dish that sells 90 plates may still be bringing in tables where one guest is vegetarian, so its value is larger than its own sales.

If there's another reason to remove it, such as kitchen time, waste or quality, state that reason. On the evidence in the paper, the risotto should stay.

## 2. The beef price rise is left out of the projection

§4 notes that beef rises **12% from 1 April**, the same day the new prices take effect. The £810 gain assumes food costs don't change.

| Dish | Food cost now | +12% if the whole plate cost is beef | Weekly cost of rise |
|---|---|---|---|
| Burger | £4.20 | +£0.50 | up to £131 |
| Sirloin | £10.40 | +£1.25 | up to £150 |

- Beef isn't the whole plate cost, so the true figure is lower. But the beef rise could take **up to about £280 a week**, a third of the projected gain.
- The steak's £2 increase barely covers its own beef rise. Its margin could fall from 60% to about **58%**, even after the price increase.

## 3. VAT is probably counted in the margins and the gain

If menu prices include 20% VAT, as is normal for UK restaurants, then:
- **The gain:** the £810 a week is VAT-inclusive. The restaurant keeps about **£675 a week (about £35,000 a year)**, not £42,000.
- **The margins:** they're calculated on VAT-inclusive prices, so they overstate true margin. On a VAT-exclusive basis, fish and chips is about 63%, not 69%.

If the 70% target and the 67% current figure are measured the same way, the trend comparison still holds. But the figures for owners should be VAT-exclusive, or labelled clearly.

## 4. The "about 71%" margin depends on both omissions

Rebuilding main-course margin from Table 1, on the same VAT-inclusive basis and with a rough assumption for specials:

| | Main-course margin |
|---|---|
| Now | about 69.5% |
| After the price rises, ignoring beef | about 71% ✓ |
| After the price rises, with the beef rise at its upper bound | about 69% |
| ... and replacing the risotto with a 64% special | about 68% |

The 71% figure is correct only if beef costs don't rise and the risotto stays.

## 5. "If volumes hold"

- **How much volume can fall before the gain disappears:** a fall of about **9%** in sales of the three repriced dishes. That figure is before beef and VAT, so the real threshold is lower. Stating it explicitly gives the owners a figure to monitor against.
- **Loyal regulars:** a 60% repeat base is a strength, but regulars are also the guests most likely to notice price changes. Loyalty doesn't mean they don't care about price.
- **Value position:** today, all three dishes are cheaper than every competitor. After the rises they sit in the middle of the range, above the cheapest competitor on each dish. That's still competitive, but no longer clearly the "value option."
- **The 2024 comparison:** "No visible effect on bookings" doesn't show volumes held. Guests can keep booking but switch to cheaper dishes.
- **Monitoring baseline:** comparing spring with January–February will pick up seasonal changes as well as any price effect. Use the same weeks last year as the baseline, or at least alongside January–February.
- **Lunch trade:** lunch is called "a small share" of sales, but not quantified.

## 6. Smaller point

The Recommendation refers to "six trading days a week." §2 says the restaurant opens Wednesday to Sunday, which is five. The weekly figures aren't affected, but the text should be consistent.

## Suggested revisions

1. **Keep the risotto,** or give a reason other than margin for removing it.
2. **Include the beef price rise** in the projection, using the actual beef share of burger and steak costs.
3. **Report gains and margins net of VAT,** or label them clearly.
4. **Revise the main-course margin figure** to reflect beef costs.
5. **Add the break-even volume figure,** and monitor against the same weeks last year as well as against January–February.
6. **Correct "six trading days."**

**Overall:** the three price rises are sensible, since current prices are below every competitor and costs are rising. But the realistic gain is closer to £25,000–£35,000 a year than £42,000, depending on beef share and VAT. The risotto proposal rests on reading the margin column backwards and should be dropped.
